notes:
I've written notes for every verse group, but some gaps are listed at the end. A few pages I read were cut off partway, so verses 7–20 rely mostly on Wesley, Matthew Henry and other older commentaries rather than Enduring Word or the Pulpit Commentary.

# Hebrews 6: Research Notes

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1 ("leave the elementary teachings… go on to maturity")**
- Guzik says "elementary principles" means the ABCs: necessary building blocks, but a foundation with nothing built on it isn't finished. The word for "perfection" is better read as "maturity," which believers can reach in this life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-6/
- The Pulpit Commentary says "let us be borne on" is the writer urging his readers to grow, not just announcing his next topic. Calling these things a foundation doesn't make them less important. The church Fathers took "dead works" to mean sinful works. "Faith in God" is deliberately not yet faith in Christ: it is the starting point a Jew and a Christian shared. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hebrews-6.html
- Wesley reads "dead works" as open sins, the first thing preachers press on hearers, with faith in God the next step. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/6.htm
- Clarke: Repentance may be properly called the foundation of the work of God in the soul of man, because by it we forsake sin, and turn to God to find mercy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-1.html
- Precept Austin points out that the chapter break hides the "Therefore," which links back to the readers' immaturity in 5:11–14. Because of their immaturity, they need to leave and stop focusing on the basics and move on to deeper truths that produce maturity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_61-3

**v. 2 (baptisms, laying on of hands, resurrection, judgment)**
- Guzik sees three pairs: repentance and faith, baptisms and laying on of hands, resurrection and judgment. He argues that almost nothing on the list is distinctively Christian. The Greek word for "baptisms" here usually means Jewish ceremonial washings, so the list is common ground the struggling readers could retreat to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-6/
- The Pulpit Commentary makes the same point about the word. It includes Jewish washings and proselyte baptism, but Christian baptism is also in view. It takes the laying on of hands as hands laid on after baptism, i.e. confirmation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hebrews-6.html
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown likewise pairs the laying on of hands with baptism. They say it answers to the rite of confirmation in Episcopal churches. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Hbr/Hbr_006.cfm
- Wesley says hands were laid on new believers so they would receive the Spirit. The judgment is called eternal, because the sentence then pronounced is irreversible, and the effects of it remain for ever. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-6.html

**v. 3 ("if God permits")**
- Guzik: this doesn't mean God might not want them to mature. It expresses complete dependence on God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-6/
- The Pulpit Commentary: they can press on *if* they are still in a state where God allows progress, because a person can slide back past the point of recovery. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hebrews-6.html
- Ligonier links v. 3 directly to vv. 4–6: Only those who have not fallen away, who have not held the Son of God up to contempt, can be restored to repentance and thus led on to maturity. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/impossible-restore
- Precept Austin sees two sides here: God's sovereignty (permits) and Man's responsibility (we will do). https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_61-3

**vv. 4–5 (enlightened, tasted, shared in the Spirit)**
- Guzik takes "impossible" at full strength. He compares the other "impossibles" in Hebrews (6:18, 10:4, 11:6). He works through each phrase. "Tasted" can mean a full experience, as when Jesus tasted death (2:9). "The heavenly gift" is probably salvation. "The powers of the age to come" means God's supernatural power. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-6/
- The Pulpit Commentary notes that the early church called baptism "enlightenment," but says the phrase means real inner light. "Tasted" means experience, not just knowledge. "Partakers" means actually sharing in the Spirit. The "powers" are the miraculous gifts, a foretaste of the Messiah's coming age. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hebrews-6.html
- A Preacher's Homiletical Commentary note reads it the other way: Enlightened — Simply instructed; the word does not imply having illumination. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-4.html

**v. 6 ("fallen away… crucifying the Son of God all over again")**
- Barnes: the Greek has no "if." It literally says "having fallen away." https://studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/hebrews-6.html
- Matthew Henry: apostates show they approve of what the Jews did in crucifying Christ, and that they would be glad to do the same thing again if it were in their power. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_006.cfm
- Guzik's reading in context: if they retreat into Judaism, no amount of religious "repentance" will help them. That retreat, especially going back to animal sacrifice, is crucifying Christ again. He separates *falling* from *falling away*: the difference between Peter and Judas. Someone who is afraid this verse condemns them shows by that very fear that it doesn't. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-6/
- The Pulpit Commentary: the verse doesn't say repentance would fail to help them. It says they cannot be brought to repentance at all. It also notes that worried believers who fear they've committed the unpardonable sin "cannot have entirely fallen from grace" if they long for pardon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hebrews-6.html
- A Biblical Illustrator writer places the impossibility on the human side: it is impossible, by any renewed course of elementary instruction, to bring back such apostates. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-4.html

**vv. 7–8 (land, rain, thorns)**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the same land gets the rain in both verses, so the failure is the land's own fault. The thorns echo the curse in Genesis 3. The land is only "near" a curse, so the writer stops short of saying his readers are already hopeless. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hebrews-6.html
- Wesley: "rejected" means No more labour is bestowed upon it. On "to be burned": As Jerusalem was shortly after. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-6.html

**v. 9 ("better things… that accompany salvation")**
- Wesley notes this is the only place the writer calls them "beloved." He reads it as We are persuaded you are now saved from your sins; and that ye have that faith, love, and holiness, which lead to final salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-6.html
- Matthew Henry: these are things that are never separated from salvation, things that show the person to be in a state of salvation, and will issue in eternal salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-13.html

**v. 10 ("God is not unjust")**
- The Pulpit Commentary: their ongoing love for fellow believers is the reason for the writer's confidence. This isn't salvation earned by merit. God in his justice is gracious to those who have used his grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hebrews-6.html

**v. 11 (diligence, "make your hope sure")**
- Wesley: full assurance of hope is something you cannot expect, if you abate your diligence. The full assurance of faith relates to present pardon; the full assurance of hope, to future glory. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-6.html
- Matthew Henry: full assurance is hope in a higher degree, and is attainable by great diligence and perseverance to the end. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_006.cfm

**v. 12 ("imitate those who… inherit")**
- Bible.org (Utley) thinks this may alude to the roll call of the faithful in chapter 11. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-6
- Wesley takes "the promises" to mean The promised rest; paradise. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-6.html

**vv. 13–15 (God's oath to Abraham)**
- Wesley says no stronger promise could have been made than the one to Abraham and in him to us. He says Abraham waited Thirty years. and received Isaac, the pledge of all the promises. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-6.html

**v. 16 (human oaths)**
- Wesley adds that this shows that an oath taken in a religious manner is lawful even under the gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-6.html
- Matthew Henry: an oath ends disputes both to disputes within our own breasts (doubts and distrusts), and disputes with others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-13.html

**vv. 17–18 (two unchangeable things)**
- Wesley: the two things are His promise and his oath. "Fled" means fled After having been tossed by many storms. The hope is On Christ, the object of our hope, and the glory we hope for through him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/6.htm
- TGC: We who are Abraham's heirs have God's promise and oath to assure us that his promised salvation is our sure hope. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/does-hebrews-6-teach-you-can-lose-your-salvation/

**v. 19 (anchor behind the curtain)**
- Guzik: the anchor was a common picture of hope in the ancient world. But the comparison isn't exact: We are anchored upward in heaven, not down in the ground; and we are anchored to move on, not to stand still. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hebrews-6/
- Matthew Henry: the anchor does not seek to fasten in the sands, but enters within the veil, and fixes there upon Christ. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Hbr/Hbr_006.cfm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown combine two pictures: the soul is the ship, hope is the anchor, and God's promise and oath are the cable connecting the ship and anchor. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-19.html
- The Biblical Illustrator gives a caution: It is only an anchor of the soul, not an anchor of the body. We must not expect from the Lord what He never promised. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-19.html

**v. 20 (forerunner, Melchizedek)**
- Wesley: a forerunner is usually less important than those who follow him, But it is not so here; for Christ who is gone before us is infinitely superior to us. On "within the veil": Thus he slides back to the priesthood of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/6.htm
- Wuest, quoted by Precept Austin: this High Priest is not in the line of Aaron, but in that of Melchisedec. He is an eternal High Priest. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_619-20

## 2. Where Protestant traditions really differ

**vv. 4–6: who is being described, and can a true believer be lost?**

- **Reformed:**
  - Ligonier gives one possible reading: the writer could be referring to apostates, to those who were members of the visible church but fell away from the faith and, thus, proved they never were part of the true church. https://www.ligonier.org/learn/devotionals/what-about-hebrews
  - Monergism (A. W. Pink): "fallen away" means a deliberate, complete, and final repudiation of Christ. https://www.monergism.com/apostasy-and-hebrews-64-6
  - TGC (2026) offers a different Reformed-friendly reading. The verse doesn't say a fallen person can't return to Christ. It insists that it's impossible to leave the new covenant, repent, and return to the life of the Mosaic administration. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/impossible-apostates-return/
- **Calvin himself:** he notes that the Novatians used this passage to refuse pardon to the fallen. That was part of why the Western church was slow to accept the letter. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-4.html
- **Baptist:**
  - Spurgeon reads it as a real but hypothetical warning: If he fall, God will lift him up again; but if he fall away, God himself cannot save him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-4.html
  - Bible.org explains his reasoning. God uses the warning to keep Christians from falling away. It then objects that you don't need to warn someone against something impossible. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-17-when-repentance-becomes-impossible-hebrews-64-8
  - John Piper, quoted by Sam Storms, says the verse doesn't mean the people who re-crucify Christ were once really justified by the blood of Jesus. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/hebrews-6:4-6-and-the-possibility-of-apostasy
  - Gill (on v. 4) argues that people God has truly enlightened are not those who fall and perish. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/hebrews/6-4.html
- **Charismatic Reformed (Sam Storms):** he answers yes to the question of whether someone can 'partake' of the Holy Spirit and yet never know Jesus in a saving way? I believe the answer to this latter question is Yes. https://www.samstorms.org/all-articles/post/hebrews-6:4-6
- **Methodist/Wesleyan:**
  - Wesley: Here is not a supposition, but a plain relation of fact. The verse describes people who lost faith, hope and love on purpose. Of these wilful total apostates he declares, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance. (though they were renewed once,) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/hebrews/6.htm
  - He reads each phrase of v. 4 as describing real conversion. "Enlightened" means by God's love in Christ. "The heavenly gift" means Remission of sins. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/hebrews-6.html
  - Barnes (a Presbyterian) also thinks it describes true Christians, but as a warning to keep them from falling. He also gives thanks that God "has" kept all his true people from apostasy. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bnb/hebrews-6.html
- **Pentecostal (Assemblies of God):**
  - The official AG position: The believer's salvation may be forfeited or abandoned by willfully turning away from Christ, and it cites Hebrews 6:4–6. https://ag.org/Beliefs/Position-Papers/Assurance-Of-Salvation
  - The AG Enrichment journal (Kowalski) links vv. 4–8 to Jesus' vine-and-branches warning in John 15. It says the risk of loss is for people who have clearly been in relationship with Christ. On whether someone can come back, it notes that "since" in v. 6 can also be translated "while": As long as someone continues to reject Christ, they cannot be renewed to repentance. https://enrichmentjournal.ag.org/Issues/2012/Summer-2012/Once-Saved-Always-Saved
- **Anglican:** the Pulpit Commentary (an Anglican work) says the experiences in vv. 4–5 are real grace. It accuses Calvin of forcing the text to fit his doctrine. It says Article XVI of the Church of England rejects both the Novatian and the predestinarian misreadings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hebrews-6.html
- **Evangelical surveys:**
  - GotQuestions gives two options that both keep eternal security. Either these are unbelievers connected with the church, or it is a hypothetical case. It admits the second view is weak because the Greek text does not contain a word equivalent to the English if. https://www.gotquestions.org/Hebrews-6.html
  - Bible.org (Utley) notes that groups who teach that believers can fall away also preach repentance and reinstatement. This text seems to depreciate this position. https://bible.org/seriespage/hebrews-6
  - F. F. Bruce, via Precept Austin: he is not questioning the perseverance of the saints; we might say that rather he is insisting that those who persevere are the true saints. https://www.preceptaustin.org/hebrews_66

**v. 2: laying on of hands**
- Gill (Baptist) describes hands laid on people moving from baptism to full church membership. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-4.html
- Coffman (Restoration Movement) ties it to the apostles' practice of giving miraculous gifts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/hebrews/6-2.html
- Anglican (Pulpit Commentary) and JFB read it as confirmation (links under v. 2 above).

## 3. Other views

**Catholic:**
- On v. 2, Catholic.com says Hebrews 6:2 is especially important because, unlike the stories in Acts, it can't be dismissed as belonging only to the apostles' time. It argues the laying on of hands must be confirmation, because ordination and healing aren't given to every Christian. https://www.catholic.com/tract/confirmation
- **Early church, on v. 6:** according to the Pulpit Commentary, Tertullian and the Novatians used the verse to refuse communion to those who lapsed under persecution. The Catholic Fathers (Ambrose, Theodoret) rejected that view and took the verse to forbid repeating baptism. The Pulpit Commentary thinks both uses miss the point. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/hebrews-6.html
- Ambrose's own anti-Novatian work, *Concerning Repentance*, is on newadvent, but the part I saw doesn't quote this verse directly. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/34061.htm

**Debated popular teaching:**
- The AG article criticises Charles Stanley's "once saved, always saved" view: in Stanley's words, God requires only an act of faith in Christ, not ongoing faith (paraphrased in the article). It also notes that MacArthur rejects that version and holds the classic Reformed view instead. This is the AG's account of Stanley, not Stanley's own page. https://enrichmentjournal.ag.org/Issues/2012/Summer-2012/Once-Saved-Always-Saved

## Not found (left out)

- Orthodox readings (oca.org)

- Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter
- Ellicott's notes
- Enduring Word and the Pulpit Commentary on the later verses: those pages cut off before vv. 7–20 and v. 11 respectively
